py-easy-76.syntax:
# General form: prefix immediately before the opening quote
# r'...'  or  R"..."  -> raw string: backslash is NOT an escape character
raw = r'text with \backslashes'

# Examples
normal = 'tab\there'      # \t becomes a real TAB character
raw_s  = r'tab\there'     # stays as backslash + 't' (9 chars)
print(len('a\nb'), len(r'a\nb'))   # 3 4

win_path = r'D:\temp\reports'      # \t and \r stay literal
pattern  = r'\d{3}-\w+'            # handy for re patterns, but it is still a plain str

# Variations
# rb'...' / br'...'  -> raw bytes literal
# rf'...' / fr'...'  -> raw f-string: {expr} still interpolated
name = 'x'
print(rf'\{name}\n')                 # \x\n

# Gotchas
# - A raw string cannot end in an odd number of backslashes:
#     r'folder\'   -> SyntaxError (the \' still escapes the quote)
#     use 'folder\\' or r'folder' + '\\'
# - r'\'' is valid and is TWO chars: backslash + quote
# - Raw only affects how the literal is parsed; the result is an ordinary str
#   (type(r'a') is str) and slashes are never converted.
# - Without r, unknown escapes like '\d' give a SyntaxWarning (3.12+).
py-easy-76.title: String literals

py-easy-78.syntax:
# General form: adjacent string literals, separated only by
# whitespace or comments, are joined at compile time
#   "part1" "part2" ...  ->  "part1part2"

greeting = "Hello, " "world"      # 'Hello, world'

# Common use: split a long string across lines inside parentheses
msg = (
    "Line one, "     # comments are allowed between parts
    "line two."
)                     # 'Line one, line two.'

# Prefixes can be mixed per part
pattern = r"\d+" "-" f"{3}"    # '\\d+-3'

# Gotchas:
# - Works only with literals, not variables or expressions:
#     a = "x"; a "y"          -> SyntaxError; use a + "y"
# - A missing comma in a list silently joins items:
#     ["red", "green" "blue"]  -> ['red', 'greenblue']
# - Cannot mix bytes and str literals: b"x" "y" -> SyntaxError
# - Across lines without parentheses you need a backslash:
#     s = "a" \
#         "b"
# - Each part keeps its own prefix: r"\n" "\n" is a raw
#   backslash-n followed by a real newline
py-easy-78.title: String literals

py-easy-79.syntax:
# General form
int(x)              # number or integer string -> int
int(s, base=10)     # parse string s in given base
float(x)            # number or numeric string -> float

# Examples
int('-17')          # -17
int(' 300 ')        # 300 (surrounding whitespace allowed)
int(9.99)           # 9   (float arg: truncates toward zero)
int(-3.7)           # -3
int('ff', 16)       # 255
int('1_000')        # 1000 (underscores allowed)

# Gotchas
# int('7.25')  -> ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10
#   A string must be an integer literal; decimal point not allowed.
# Convert via float first:  int(float('7.25'))  -> 7
# int('') / int('abc') -> ValueError
# int(None) -> TypeError
# Truncation is toward zero; use math.floor() / round() for other rounding.
# int('0x1A', 0) -> 26  (base 0 infers prefix 0x/0o/0b)
py-easy-79.title: Built-in type conversion

py-easy-80.syntax:
# General form
float(x)        # x: str, int, float, or object with __float__/__index__
float()         # -> 0.0

# Examples
float('\t-2.5e3\n')   # -2500.0  (leading/trailing whitespace is stripped)
float(7)              # 7.0
float(' inf ')        # inf
float('-Infinity')    # -inf
float('nan')          # nan
float('1_000.25')     # 1000.25 (underscores allowed between digits)

# Gotchas
# float('2 .5')    -> ValueError (internal whitespace not allowed)
# float('')        -> ValueError
# float('1,5')     -> ValueError (no comma decimals; use locale.atof)
# float('0x1A')    -> ValueError (use float.fromhex('0x1Ap0') or int(s, 16))
# float(None)      -> TypeError
# int(' 42 ')      -> 42 (int also strips surrounding whitespace)
# int('4.2')       -> ValueError; use int(float('4.2')) -> 4
# Result is a float, not a str: repr shows 2.5, not '2.5'
# Case-insensitive specials: 'NaN', 'INF', 'infinity' all accepted
py-easy-80.title: Built-in type conversions

py-easy-81.syntax:
# General form: any object can be evaluated in a boolean context
bool(obj)        # explicit conversion -> True or False
if obj: ...      # implicit truth test (also while, and/or/not)

# Falsy values: None, False, numeric zeros, empty containers
bool(None)       # False
bool(0.0)        # False
bool(0j)         # False
bool('')         # False  (empty string)
bool([]), bool({}), bool(set()), bool(range(0))  # all False

# Everything else is truthy, including non-empty strings
bool('False')    # True  - content doesn't matter, only length
bool(' ')        # True  - a single space is non-empty
bool([None])     # True  - list with one element

# Gotchas:
# - Strings are truthy iff len(s) > 0; text like 'no' or '0.0' is still True
# - Convert first if you mean the number: bool(int('7')), bool(float('0.0'))
# - Custom classes: __bool__ is used, else __len__, else always True
# - and/or return an operand, not a bool: '' or 'default' -> 'default'
py-easy-81.title: Built-in types and boolean contexts

py-easy-86.syntax:
# Arithmetic errors: raised by numeric operations that cannot produce a result
# Hierarchy: Exception -> ArithmeticError -> ZeroDivisionError / OverflowError / FloatingPointError

try:
    result = 10 % 0          # also applies to /, //, %, divmod()
except ZeroDivisionError as exc:
    print(type(exc).__name__, exc)   # ZeroDivisionError integer modulo by zero

# Catching the base class also catches its subclasses
try:
    total = 7.5 // 0.0
except ArithmeticError as exc:
    print("caught:", type(exc).__name__)   # caught: ZeroDivisionError

# Gotchas:
# - Float division by zero also raises; Python does not return inf for 5.0 / 0.0
# - float('inf') arithmetic is fine: float('inf') / 2 -> inf
# - math.inf * 0 -> nan (no exception)
# - Decimal(3) / 0 raises decimal.DivisionByZero (subclass of ZeroDivisionError)
# - ValueError is for bad argument values, e.g. int('abc') or math.sqrt(-1)
# - 0 ** -1 raises ZeroDivisionError too
py-easy-86.title: Built-in exceptions

py-easy-88.syntax:
# General form
# int(x)            -> convert a number or numeric string to int
# int(x, base=10)   -> parse a string/bytes in the given base

# Examples
int("42")          # 42
int("  -7 ")       # -7  (surrounding whitespace allowed)
int("1_000")       # 1000 (underscores allowed like literals)
int("ff", 16)      # 255
int(3.9)           # 3   (truncates toward zero)

# Right type, bad value  -> ValueError
try:
    int("xyz")
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)       # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'xyz'

# Wrong type entirely    -> TypeError
try:
    int([1, 2])
except TypeError as e:
    print(e)       # int() argument must be a string, ... not 'list'

# Gotchas
# int("3.5")  -> ValueError (use int(float("3.5")))
# int("")     -> ValueError
# int(None)   -> TypeError
# Errors happen at runtime, never SyntaxError: the string is data, not code.
# ValueError = argument has the right type but an inappropriate value.
# TypeError  = operation applied to an object of an inappropriate type.
py-easy-88.title: Built-in exceptions and type conversion

py-easy-89.syntax:
# General form
raise ExceptionClass("message")   # create and throw immediately
raise                              # inside except: re-raise current exception
raise NewError("msg") from err     # chain exceptions

# Example: signal invalid state
def withdraw(balance, amount):
    if amount > balance:
        raise RuntimeError(f"insufficient funds: {amount}")
    return balance - amount

# Example: catch it
try:
    withdraw(10, 50)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("caught:", e)        # caught: insufficient funds: 50

# Gotchas / variations:
# - raise stops normal flow at once; the exception propagates up the call
#   stack until a matching except handles it, else the program ends with
#   a traceback.
# - Works anywhere, not only inside try blocks.
# - Creating an exception object without raise does nothing:
#   err = KeyError("x")   # no effect until `raise err`
# - raise KeyError (the class) is allowed; Python instantiates it.
# - Only BaseException subclasses can be raised; raise "text" -> TypeError.
# - warnings.warn() is for non-fatal warnings, not raise.
py-easy-89.title: Exceptions and error handling

py-easy-90.syntax:
# General form: put script-only code under the module name check
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # runs only when this file is executed directly
    ...

# Example: greet.py
def greet(who):
    return f"Hello, {who}!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    print(greet(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "world"))

# $ python greet.py Ada      -> __name__ is "__main__", prints Hello, Ada!
# >>> import greet           -> __name__ is "greet", nothing printed
# >>> greet.greet("Bo")      -> 'Hello, Bo!'

# Common pattern: return an exit code from a function
def run():
    print("working")
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(run())

# Gotchas:
# - Python has no required entry-point function; the name main() is only a convention.
# - Module-level code outside the guard still runs on import.
# - python -m pkg.mod also sets __name__ to "__main__".
# - For a package, python -m pkg runs pkg/__main__.py.
# - Repeated imports reuse the cached module from sys.modules; the guard does not cause this.
py-easy-90.title: Modules and script execution

py-easy-92.syntax:
# Assignment anywhere in a function body makes that name local
# for the WHOLE function (decided at compile time).
total = 10

def add_bonus():
    total = total + 5   # UnboundLocalError: local 'total' read before assignment

# Reading only (no assignment) uses the enclosing/global value:
def show():
    print(total)        # 10

# Declare global to rebind the module-level name:
def add_bonus():
    global total
    total = total + 5   # module-level total becomes 15

# nonlocal rebinds a name in the nearest enclosing function:
def outer():
    hits = 0
    def bump():
        nonlocal hits
        hits += 1
    bump()
    return hits         # 1

# Gotchas:
# - Augmented assignment (x += 1) also counts as assignment -> local.
# - UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError.
# - Mutating a global object (items.append(3)) needs no 'global';
#   only rebinding the name does.
# - Lookup order: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in (LEGB).
py-easy-92.title: Variable scope

py-easy-94.syntax:
# General form: defaults are used for any parameter not supplied
def func(pos, opt1=default1, opt2=default2):
    ...

# Arguments can be passed by position or by keyword (name=value)
def greet(name, greeting="Hi", punct="!"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}{punct}"

greet("Ann")                  # 'Hi, Ann!'      (both defaults used)
greet("Ann", "Hey")           # 'Hey, Ann!'     (positional fills greeting)
greet("Ann", punct="?")       # 'Hi, Ann?'      (skip greeting, set punct by name)
greet(punct=".", name="Bo")   # 'Hi, Bo.'       (keyword order doesn't matter)

# Gotchas:
# - Keyword args may skip over earlier defaulted parameters.
# - Positional args must come before keyword args in a call:
#     greet(name="Ann", "Hey")    -> SyntaxError
# - Supplying the same parameter twice is an error:
#     greet("Ann", name="Bo")     -> TypeError: multiple values
# - Parameters without defaults cannot follow ones with defaults in a def.
# - Default values are evaluated once at def time; avoid mutable defaults
#   like [] -- use None and create the list inside the function.
# - Use * in the def to force keyword-only params: def g(a, *, b=1)
py-easy-94.title: Function arguments

py-easy-95.syntax:
# General form: positional args fill parameters left to right;
# keyword args match parameters by name, in any order.
def func(p1, p2, p3=default): ...
func(v1, v2)            # positional: p1=v1, p2=v2
func(p2=v2, p1=v1)      # keyword: order doesn't matter
func(v1, p3=x, p2=v2)   # mix: positionals first, then keywords

# Example
def describe(animal, sound):
    return f"{animal} says {sound}"

describe('cat', 'meow')               # 'cat says meow'
describe(sound='meow', animal='cat')  # same result
describe(animal='meow', sound='cat')  # 'meow says cat' (names decide)

# Gotchas:
# - Positional args cannot follow keyword args:
#     describe(animal='cat', 'meow')  -> SyntaxError
# - Giving a parameter twice raises TypeError:
#     describe('cat', animal='dog')   -> TypeError
# - Bare names are variables, not strings:
#     describe(cat, meow)  -> NameError if undefined
# - Force keyword-only with *:  def f(a, *, b): ...
# - Force positional-only with /: def f(a, /, b): ...
py-easy-95.title: Function calls and arguments

py-easy-97.syntax:
# General form: return several values as a tuple, unpack at the call site
def func(args):
    return value1, value2        # same as: return (value1, value2)

a, b = func(args)                # tuple unpacking into two names

# Example
def divmod_pair(x, y):
    return x // y, x % y

q, r = divmod_pair(17, 5)       # q == 3, r == 2

# Keep the whole tuple instead
pair = divmod_pair(17, 5)       # pair == (3, 2)
pair[0], pair[1]                # index access also works

# Variations
first, *rest = (10, 20, 30)     # first == 10, rest == [20, 30]
_, r = divmod_pair(9, 4)        # ignore a value with _
(a, b), c = (1, 2), 3           # nested unpacking

# Gotchas
# - Number of names must match the number of items:
#     a, b = (1, 2, 3)  -> ValueError: too many values to unpack
# - Lists and any other iterable unpack the same way as tuples
# - The comma makes the tuple, not the parentheses: return 1, is (1,)
py-easy-97.title: Functions and return values

py-easy-98.syntax:
# General form: assignment binds a name to an object; it never copies
name_b = name_a          # both names now refer to the SAME object

# Example: aliasing a mutable object
scores = {'amy': 7}
alias = scores
alias['bob'] = 9
print(scores)            # {'amy': 7, 'bob': 9}
print(alias is scores)   # True (same identity)

# Making an independent (shallow) copy instead
nums = [10, 20]
copy1 = nums.copy()      # or nums[:] or list(nums)
copy1.append(30)
print(nums)              # [10, 20]  unchanged

# Gotchas:
# - Rebinding is not mutation: alias = {} makes alias point elsewhere;
#   scores is unaffected.
# - Immutable objects (int, str, tuple) can't change in place, so
#   x = y; x += 1 rebinds x and y keeps its value.
# - For lists, x += [..] mutates in place (like extend), unlike x = x + [..].
# - Shallow copies share nested objects; use copy.deepcopy() for
#   fully independent nested structures.
# - Mutable default arguments (def f(a=[])) are shared across calls.
# - Use 'is' to check identity, '==' to check equality.
py-easy-98.title: Variables and mutable objects
